planting.note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; unlike the spring-blooming atamasco lily, Simpson's rain lily is a fall-flowering Gulf Coast native that opens its blooms after the first cool, rainy fronts of autumn.

directions: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Simpson's rain lily is native to wet pine flatwoods, prairies, and roadside ditches of the Florida panhandle and adjacent Gulf Coast, where it was long confused with the similar spring-blooming atamasco lily before being recognized as a distinct, later-flowering species. Its solitary white flowers, often lightly flushed pink on the outside of the petals, open in autumn rather than spring, triggered by the same cooling rains that bring on fall wildflower displays across the coastal plain. It naturalizes well at the sunny to lightly shaded edge of a wet meadow or rain garden, where the strappy foliage stays low and unobtrusive until the surprise of fall bloom. All parts are toxic if eaten, so site it away from areas where pets or children graze on plants.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer to early fall in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, setting the rhizome shallowly at or just below the surface; prairie iris grows naturally in open wet savannas and pine flatwoods rather than the deep marsh favored by other Louisiana iris species, so it tolerates a somewhat less saturated garden spot.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer or early fall in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, setting the rhizome shallowly with its top at or just below the surface. Prairie iris is the most recently recognized of the Louisiana iris species, native to open, fire-maintained wet savannas and pine flatwoods across the Gulf Coastal Plain from Louisiana to the Florida panhandle, distinguished from its wetland relatives by its smaller, more compact stature and preference for seasonally moist rather than permanently flooded ground. Its blue-violet flowers, carried on branched stalks above narrow sword-shaped leaves, open in mid-spring and draw bumblebees and swallowtails. Because it comes from open, sunny habitat, it tolerates more direct sun than copper or giant blue iris and suits a wet meadow planting or the damp, sunny margin of a rain garden as well as a shadier pond edge.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring in consistently moist, acidic soil in partial to full shade; slender woodoats is native to wet pine savannas, bog margins, and swamp edges across the southeastern coastal plain and, unlike its larger relative inland sea oats, wants steadier moisture and tolerates less drying between rains.

directions: Direct sow in consistently moist, acidic soil in partial to full shade; slender woodoats is a smaller, more delicate southeastern relative of the better-known inland sea oats, native to wet pine savannas, bog edges, and swamp-margin woods from Virginia to Texas. It forms a low, fine-textured clump of narrow blades topped in summer by slender, nodding spikelets, lighter and airier than the broader, more pendulous seed clusters of Chasmanthium latifolium, and it persists into winter as a soft tan accent. Because it comes from consistently damp, acidic ground, it performs best at a pond margin, rain garden, or the wet, shaded edge of a bog planting rather than an average shade border, and it does not tolerate the same periodic drying that inland sea oats shrugs off. Self-sows modestly in favorable conditions; thin volunteer seedlings where a tidier clump is wanted.
